text: On Racetrack Playa, a flat, dry lakebed in Death Valley, California, rocks lie at the ends of long tracks carved into the cracked mud. Some trails run straight, some zigzag, and some rocks seem to have turned around. For about 70 years, people argued about how they moved.

In 2013 and 2014, a team of scientists finally watched it happen. After a rare rain, a shallow pond forms on the playa and freezes at night. On sunny mornings, the ice cracks into thin, floating panes, some tens of metres across. A light breeze pushes these panes, and they bulldoze the rocks slowly across the slippery mud.

st.reveal: After a rare winter rain, a shallow pond forms and freezes overnight. On sunny mornings the ice breaks into big thin panes. A light breeze pushes the panes, and they shove the rocks across the soft mud.

sec.t:
Death Valley is one of the [[@hot-places|hottest places]] on Earth. In 1913, a thermometer there recorded 56.7°C, the highest air temperature ever officially measured, although some experts doubt that reading. Not far away, Badwater Basin sits 86 metres below sea level, the lowest point in North America.

Racetrack Playa is higher and cooler, about 1,130 m up. It is roughly 4.5 km long and almost perfectly flat, so flat that from a distance it looks like a frozen lake. Rocks fall onto it from the surrounding hills, and then, somehow, they travel.

In 2011, a team including the cousins Richard and James Norris got permission to place rocks fitted with [[@gps-how|GPS]] trackers on the playa. They also set up a weather station and time-lapse cameras. Then they waited.

In December 2013, they got lucky. A thin pond, just a few centimetres deep, had frozen. As the sun rose, the ice, only 3 to 6 mm thick, broke into large panes. A breeze of about 3 to 5 metres a second pushed them along, and rocks all across the playa began to move. One travelled about 224 metres.

The team had been ready to wait five or ten years for a single move. Instead, the big day came after about two, and dozens of rocks moved within minutes of each other.

sec.h: Why ice makes such a good sail
sec.t:
A heavy rock sits firmly on dry mud. [[@friction|Friction]], the gripping force between surfaces, holds it in place. But a wide sheet of ice catches a lot of wind, like a sail on a boat. Floating on water, it slides with almost no [[friction|friction]], and it pushes against the rock with the combined force of the wind on the whole sheet.

The soft wet mud underneath keeps a perfect record. The rock's bottom scratches a groove, and when the water dries away, the trail stays for years.

The National Park Service does not allow visitors to take rocks or drive on the playa. Car tyres leave scars that can last for decades, because the playa may only get a little rain each year to smooth them out.

Similar moving rocks have been found on a few other dry lakes in Nevada and elsewhere. And rocks are not the only things that seem to move without legs: some [[@plants-move|plants]] can track the sun or snap shut in a fraction of a second.

text: The Thar, or Great Indian Desert, covers much of western Rajasthan and stretches into Pakistan. It is dry mainly because of where it sits and [[@wind-patterns|how the winds blow]].

The Thar lies in a belt of the planet, north of the tropics, where sinking dry air is common. When the southwest [[@monsoon|monsoon]] arrives, one branch of it blows in from the Arabian Sea. But nothing forces that moist air to rise over the Thar. The Aravalli hills run alongside the winds instead of across them, so the clouds pass over and drop their rain further away, in the Himalayan foothills and beyond.
Hot, dusty air over the desert also makes clouds less likely to form. The result is a land where some places get less than 100 mm of rain in a year.

st.reveal: Rain falls when moist air is forced to rise and cool. The Aravallis lie roughly southwest to northeast, the same way the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon blows. The winds slide along them instead of climbing over, and carry their moisture away.

sec.t:
Scientists are still piecing together the Thar's history. Studies of buried sand layers suggest that dry, dune-building periods came and went over hundreds of thousands of years, as Earth swung between ice ages and warmer times. When the monsoon weakened, the desert spread. When it grew stronger, lakes filled and grass grew.

Along the desert's northern edge runs the [[@mystery-lost-saraswati|dry bed of the Ghaggar-Hakra river]]. Several cities of the [[@indus-cities|Indus civilisation]], such as Kalibangan in Rajasthan, stood near it. Many experts think the river carried more water in the past, but how much, and when it dried, is still debated.

The Thar is one of the most crowded deserts on Earth. People have lived here for thousands of years by being clever with water. Villages dug [[@india-wonder-rani-ki-vav|stepwells]] and built small covered tanks, called kundis, to catch every drop of rain. Herders raise [[@camels|camels]], goats and sheep that can cope with heat and [[drought|drought]].

The Bishnoi community has protected khejri trees and blackbuck for centuries. Their story of the people of Khejarli, who gave their lives to save trees in 1730, is still told across India. [[@desert-life|Life in the desert]], from music to food to building, shows how much people can do with very little.

The biggest change came with the Indira Gandhi Canal. Work started in 1958, and it now carries water from the Himalayan rivers of [[@punjab|Punjab]] hundreds of kilometres into the desert. Farms of wheat, mustard and cotton have sprung up where there were once only dunes.

The canal brought food and jobs, but also new problems. In some areas, water has soaked in and raised salt to the surface, making the soil harder to farm. Desert animals like the great Indian bustard, a bird as tall as a small child, have lost much of their [[@grasslands|open grassland]], and only a small number of them survive.

text: No. Mushrooms belong to their own group of living things, the [[fungus|fungi]]. For a long time scientists filed them with plants, because both stay in one place and grow out of soil. Then they looked closer.

Plants are green because they use sunlight to build their food. Fungi have no green colour and cannot do this at all. Instead they grow into dead leaves, wood or soil, release juices that break the food down outside their bodies, and soak it up. [[dna|DNA]] studies show that fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. So the mushroom on your pizza is, in a family-tree sense, nearer to you than to the tomato under it.

sec.h: The mushroom is only the tip

sec.t:
Without fungi, forests would be buried under their own fallen leaves and logs. Fungi are among the few living things that can break down tough wood, returning its goodness to the soil. That is why a fallen tree in a damp forest crumbles within years.

Most land plants also team up with fungi underground. The fungus wraps around or grows into the roots and passes the plant water and minerals. In return, the plant feeds it sugar. Popular books describe a "wood wide web" where trees share food and warn each other through these threads. The partnership is real, but how much trees really talk through it is still argued over. In 2023, a team of forest scientists reviewed the studies and warned that many of the boldest claims go well beyond the evidence.

Some animals grow fungi on purpose. Leafcutter [[@ants-farm|ants]] in the Americas and many [[@termite-mounds|termites]] in India raise fungus gardens inside their nests. After the first [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains, large edible mushrooms called *Termitomyces* push up from Indian termite mounds, and villagers collect them as a seasonal treat.

A few mushrooms even glow in the dark. In 2018, scientists found a new glowing [[species|species]] growing on bamboo in [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], and they described it two years later. Its light comes from [[@bioluminescence|bioluminescence]], the same chemistry that lights up [[@fireflies|fireflies]].

Tiny single-celled fungi called [[@food-science-bread-rise|yeasts]] help make [[@wheat-bread|bread]] rise, and they play a part in [[@fermentation|fermenting]] many foods. A blue-green mould gave us penicillin, one of the first [[@antibiotics|antibiotics]], after Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that it killed [[bacteria|bacteria]] on a dish in his lab.

Mushrooms such as button, oyster and shiitake are farmed and safe to cook. Wild ones are a different story. Each year, people in India and the USA fall sick after picking mushrooms that looked harmless. Experts who know fungi well still check spores and other tiny details under a [[microscope|microscope]] before eating anything they find. Some of the most dangerous species, such as the death cap, look plain and harmless, and the illness can take hours to begin. For everyone else, the safe rule is simple: enjoy wild mushrooms with your eyes and a camera.

text: To freeze ice cream, you need something colder than 0 °C. That is because sugar in the cream mix lowers its freezing point to about minus 2 or 3 °C. Plain ice, sitting at around 0 °C, isn't cold enough to do the job.

Adding salt to the ice changes everything. Salt makes the ice melt, and melting soaks up heat. The salty slush can get as cold as about minus 21 °C. Packed around a metal tub of cream, it pulls heat out of the cream fast, and the mixture freezes.

st.reveal: Salt makes ice melt even below 0 °C. Melting needs energy, so the ice pulls heat out of its surroundings and the salty slush becomes much colder than plain ice.

sec.t:
When water freezes, its tiny particles line up into a neat pattern called a [[crystal|crystal]]. Sugar and other [[dissolve|dissolved]] things get in the way, so the water has to be colder before it can line up. Scientists call this freezing point depression.

That's handy for ice cream. A mix that froze at 0 °C would turn into a solid block. Because of the sugar, part of the water stays liquid even in a freezer, which is why good ice cream is soft enough to scoop.

In 1843 Nancy Johnson of Philadelphia patented a hand-cranked ice cream freezer. A metal can full of cream sat inside a wooden bucket packed with ice and rock salt. Turning a handle spun a paddle inside the can. Makers used coarse rock salt, whose big chunks dissolve slowly and keep the bucket cold for longer.

The stirring did two jobs. It kept scraping frozen cream off the cold walls so new cream could touch them. It also beat in air and kept the ice crystals small, making the ice cream smooth. Machines like this made [[@ice-cream|ice cream]] a treat American families could make at home on summer weekends.

Long before electric freezers, Indian kulfi makers used the same trick. They poured thick, sweet milk into small cone-shaped moulds and packed them in a big earthen pot, or matka, filled with ice and salt. Then they turned the moulds slowly until the kulfi set. Kulfi isn't churned, so it freezes dense and creamy rather than fluffy.

The [[@mughals|Mughals]] prized cold treats. Records from Emperor Akbar's court describe cooling drinking water with saltpetre, a different salt that also chills water when it dissolves. Ice was sometimes carried down from the hills to the plains.

Today most ice cream is made in big electric freezers, and a home [[@refrigerator|refrigerator]] does the cooling with a pump instead of salt. But hand-cranked and salt-and-ice methods are still used for fun, at fairs and at street kulfi stalls.

The coldest salty slush, at around minus 21 °C, is far below anything plain ice can reach. On the [[@temperature-scales|Fahrenheit scale]] used in the US, that is about minus 6 °F. A Dutch-German scientist named Daniel Fahrenheit is said to have used salt, ice and water to set the zero on his thermometer, in the early 1700s.

text: Modern art is a name for art made roughly between the 1860s and the 1970s, when many artists stopped trying to make pictures look like real life. Instead they experimented with colour, shape, feelings and ideas.

One big reason was the camera. Once [[@photography-history|photography]] could capture a face or a landscape exactly, painters no longer needed to. They began asking new questions. Can a painting show a feeling? Can it show a face from every side at once? Can it be just colour, with nothing recognisable at all? Their answers often looked strange to people at the time. Many still do.

sec.t:
For hundreds of years European art schools taught artists to use [[@perspective|perspective]], careful shading and realistic detail. The [[@impressionism|Impressionists]] began to loosen those rules in the 1870s, with quick brushstrokes and bright colour.

Others went much further. [[@van-gogh|Vincent van Gogh]] used colour to express emotion. Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque broke objects into flat, angular pieces in a style called Cubism. Each new group pushed a little harder, and audiences often reacted with laughter or anger.

In 1917 Marcel Duchamp sent a shop-bought urinal, turned on its side and signed "R. Mutt", to an exhibition in New York. He called it *Fountain*. The exhibition refused to show it. Duchamp's point was that an artist's idea and choice could matter more than skill with a brush.

People are still arguing about that idea. Some think it opened art to anyone with something to say. Others think it let people call almost anything art. Both views are reasonable, and the debate is part of what modern art is about.

In India, modern art grew alongside the freedom movement. [[@amrita-sher-gil|Amrita Sher-Gil]] blended European training with Indian subjects in the 1930s. In 1947, the year of independence, young painters in Bombay formed the Progressive Artists' Group. They included [[@mf-husain|M.F. Husain]], F.N. Souza and [[@sh-raza|S.H. Raza]].

Raza later became famous for paintings built around the *bindu*, a dot or circle that in Indian thought can stand for the starting point of everything. His work is abstract, but it grows from Indian ideas, which shows that modern art did not belong to Europe alone.

Modern art can feel confusing because it does not always try to show something. A good start is to ask simple questions. What colours did the artist choose? Does the picture feel calm, angry or joyful? What would change if one shape were moved?

Many museums, like the Museum of Modern Art in New York, which opened in 1929, put labels beside each work to explain what the artist was trying to do. Even so, you are allowed not to like something. Most modern artists expected people to argue.

text: The veena is a large string instrument from India. The kind most people mean today, the Saraswati veena, is used in South Indian Carnatic music. It has a big round wooden body, a long neck with 24 frets, and a second, smaller round shape near the top.

The player sits cross-legged with the veena held across the body, the big bowl resting on the floor or lap. She plucks the strings with her right hand and presses them against the frets with her left. Its deep, rich voice can slide smoothly from note to note, almost like singing.

sec.t:
A Saraswati veena is usually made from [[@jackfruit|jackfruit]] wood. Its main bowl, the *kudam*, is often hollowed from a single block. The neck, frets and decorations are added by hand. The town of Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu is especially famous for veena makers, and its veenas have special legal protection as a regional craft.

The frets are thin brass strips set into a ridge of black wax. Makers move them, little by little, until each note sounds right. A finished veena is about 1.2 metres long, roughly as long as a ten-year-old is tall.

A veena has four main strings for playing melody. Three thinner strings run along the side. These are plucked with the little finger to mark the [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] and to give a steady background note, called a drone.

The hollow wooden body works like a loudspeaker. The vibrating strings shake the wood, and the wood pushes far more air than a string alone could, making the sound fuller.

In Hindu tradition, Saraswati, the goddess of learning and music, is shown playing the veena. The sage Narada also carries one in many stories. The painter Raja Ravi Varma made a famous picture of Saraswati with her veena, copied in prints across India.

The word itself is ancient. In old texts, *vina* meant many kinds of string instruments, including harps. A gold coin of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta, from about 1,700 years ago, shows him seated and playing a harp-like vina. See [[@gupta-golden-age|the Gupta age]].

North India has its own veena, the *rudra veena*. It has a long tube of wood or [[@bamboo|bamboo]] with two large gourds underneath, and makes a deep, slow sound. It is used in *dhrupad*, one of the oldest styles of Hindustani music.

Very few musicians play the rudra veena today, and teachers worry it could fade away. The Saraswati veena, though, is still learned by thousands of children in South India and in Indian communities from [[@chennai|Chennai]] to New Jersey.

text: The Reserve Bank of India, or RBI, tries to keep inflation near 4% because that is low enough to protect people's money, but not so low that the economy stalls. Inflation means the general rise in prices over a year, as the story of [[@inflation|why prices go up]] explains.
The law gives the RBI a target of 4%, with a safe band from 2% to 6%. When inflation goes above 6%, as it did in October 2026, the RBI usually raises interest rates to cool things down.

news.h: Price rises cross the RBI's 6% limit for the first time in two years
news.t: On 12 November 2026, the government said retail inflation in October was 6.09%, up from 5.54% in September and the highest in two years. That is above 6%, the top of the safe band the Reserve Bank of India must aim for. Food prices rose 8.94% in a year, and onions cost more than twice as much as a year earlier. The RBI had already raised its main interest rate, the repo rate, by 0.25 percentage points to 5.50% in October, its first rise in nearly four years, and economists expected another rise at its December meeting. This entry explains why the RBI aims for 4% and how it tries to get there.

myth: When inflation is 6%, every price has gone up by 6%.

Inflation is an average over hundreds of goods and services. Some prices, like onions in a bad season, may double, while others, like phones, may even fall. The 6% is the overall change compared with a year earlier.

sec.t:
First, India has to measure inflation. Every month, government workers note the prices of hundreds of things, from rice, milk and onions to bus fares, school fees, medicines and haircuts, in cities and villages across the country. Using [[statistics|statistics]], these are combined into one number called the Consumer Price Index. Things families spend more on, like food, count for more in the average. The yearly change in this index is the inflation rate, written as a [[@percentages|percentage]].

Then the RBI acts, mainly through the repo rate. This is the [[interest|interest]] rate at which the RBI lends money to banks for short periods.

1. **Prices rise too fast.** The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, a group of six people, raises the repo rate.
2. **Banks follow.** Borrowing from the RBI costs banks more, so they charge more on [[@money-interest-loans|loans]] for homes, cars and businesses, and often pay more on savings.
3. **Spending slows.** People borrow and buy a little less, and companies expand more carefully.
4. **Prices cool.** With less rush to buy, shops and makers raise prices more slowly.

When inflation is too low and the [[economy|economy]] is weak, the RBI does the opposite and cuts the repo rate.

It works a bit like the regulator on a gas stove. Turn it up and things heat faster. Turn it down and they cool. But the change is slow, so the RBI has to guess where prices will be months ahead.

Zero might sound perfect, but a little inflation is healthy. If prices were falling, people might wait to buy, hoping things get cheaper, and businesses would struggle. Workers' wages are also hard to cut, so a gentle rise in prices gives the economy room to adjust.

On the other hand, high inflation hurts. It eats away the value of savings and hits poor families hardest, because so much of their money goes on food and fuel. Experts chose 4% for India as a middle path for a fast-growing country, while many rich countries aim for 2%.

For several years after 2016, inflation mostly stayed inside the band, though it jumped during the [[pandemic|pandemic]] and when food or fuel prices spiked. In late 2025, inflation fell very low, then began climbing again in 2026.

By October 2026, a weak [[monsoon|monsoon]] had hurt crops, and a war in West Asia earlier in the year had made oil much dearer. Food prices rose 8.94% in a year. Onions cost more than double, and garlic, ginger and lemons jumped too. Overall inflation reached 6.09%, above the top of the band for the first time in two years.

The RBI had already raised the repo rate to 5.50% in October 2026, its first increase in nearly four years, and signalled it might go further.

- **4%**: India's inflation target, with a safe band of 2% to 6%.
- **6.09%**: inflation in October 2026, just over the top of that band.
- **8.94%**: food inflation in October 2026. Food matters most for poorer families.
- **6 members**: the Monetary Policy Committee, three from the RBI and three experts named by the government.
- **12 years versus 18 years**: roughly how long prices take to double at 6% and at 4% inflation.

Raising interest rates can slow inflation, but it also makes home loans and business loans costlier, which can slow growth and jobs. Some economists say the RBI must act firmly to protect savers and the poor. Others say much of today's inflation comes from weather and world events, like a poor harvest or costly oil, which higher interest rates cannot fix. They argue that better storage, transport and [[@supply-demand|supply]] would help more.

There is also debate about the target itself. Some think 4% is right for India. Others suggest a slightly different target or band.

**"The RBI decides the price of onions."** It does not set any shop price. It can only influence how much people borrow and spend.

**"Inflation of 6% means prices rose 6% this month."** It compares prices with the same month a year earlier.

**"Low inflation means prices are falling."** Low inflation means prices are rising slowly. Falling prices are called deflation.

Inflation decides how much your family's money can buy. If your pocket money stays the same but prices rise 6%, you can buy a little less each year. When the RBI raises rates, a family with a home loan may pay a bigger monthly instalment, while savers may earn more on fixed deposits.

Learning how [[@maths-money-compound|money grows with interest]] and [[@money-banks|what banks do with your money]] helps you see why one number, announced each month, is watched by everyone from shopkeepers to the government.

text: Healthcare is expensive. A single heart operation can cost more than a family earns in a year. So most countries try to share the cost, so that people don't have to pay everything themselves at the moment they fall ill.

There are three main ways. A country can pay for care through [[@taxes|taxes]], as Britain does. It can make people and employers pay into [[@insurance|insurance funds]], as Germany does. Or people can buy their own insurance or pay at the clinic, which happens a lot in India and the USA. Most countries mix all three. The World Health Organization calls the goal "universal health coverage": everyone getting the care they need without being pushed into [[@sustainable-goals|poverty]].

st.reveal: In the USA, about half the population is covered through an employer's insurance plan. In the UK, the NHS is paid for mostly by taxes, and in Canada each province runs a public insurance plan.

sec.t:
Insurance is a way of pooling risk. Picture a thousand families each paying a small amount into a fund every year. Most of them stay healthy, but a few need costly treatment, and the fund pays for them. Nobody knows in advance who will need it, so everyone is protected.

The maths behind this is [[@probability|probability]]. Insurers estimate how many people are likely to fall ill and set the price so the fund doesn't run dry.

India has free government hospitals and health centres, but many are crowded, and lots of families choose private clinics. For years, a large share of health spending came straight out of people's pockets. A serious illness could push a family into debt.

In 2018, India launched Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, which covers hospital treatment up to ₹5 lakh per family per year for poorer households. In 2024 it was opened to everyone aged 70 and above. Many states also run their own schemes.

Other countries offer different models. Canada's public insurance grew from a plan started in the province of Saskatchewan in 1962. [[@thailand|Thailand]] brought in universal coverage in 2002, and for years a hospital visit there cost just 30 baht, less than a US dollar. For older people, health costs and [[@pensions-old-age|pensions]] are often planned together, because both grow as a population ages.

The USA has no single national system. About half of Americans get insurance through their job. Since 1965, the government programme Medicare has covered people aged 65 and over, and Medicaid helps many people with low incomes. A 2010 law, often called Obamacare, helped millions more buy insurance.

Even so, about 8% of Americans had no health insurance in 2023. Americans disagree about how far the government should go. Some want a single public plan like Canada's, while others prefer private choice. Every country is still adjusting the balance between cost, choice and fairness.

text: Most cities grow on their own, one house and lane at a time. Planning is the job of deciding ahead of time where things should go: homes, roads, schools, parks, markets, factories, water pipes and drains.

City planners study maps, count how many people live in each area and guess how many will come in the next twenty years. Then they draw a master plan. It says which land is for housing, which is for shops and offices, and where the next bus route, hospital or [[@metro-trains|metro line]] should be built.

Some cities are planned from the very first brick. Most are planned in patches, long after people have already moved in. That is much harder, a bit like rearranging the furniture while the whole family is still sitting on it.

st.prompt: A busy road keeps jamming, so the city doubles the number of lanes. What usually happens a few years later?

options.t: The road fills up with traffic again
Traffic jams disappear for good
People stop using cars altogether

st.reveal: Wider roads make driving easier, so more people choose to drive and new homes and shops spring up nearby. Planners call this "induced demand". It is one reason many cities now build metro lines and bus lanes as well as roads.

New lanes often attract more drivers, and the jams come back. Good public transport, footpaths, cycle lanes and homes close to jobs tend to work better over time.

sec.t:
Planning is old. In the [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley cities]], such as Mohenjo-daro, streets ran in straight lines that met at right angles. Covered brick drains ran along them, carrying waste water away from homes. That was about 4,500 years ago.

Jaipur, founded in 1727 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, was laid out in rectangular blocks with wide markets, guided by old Indian ideas about building. In the USA, the French-born engineer Pierre L'Enfant drew up the plan for Washington, D.C. in 1791, with broad avenues that fan out from the Capitol. In 1811, New York decided that most of Manhattan would become a giant grid of numbered streets.

sec.h: The hidden half of a plan
sec.t:
Much of a city's plan is invisible. Pipes bring in clean water. [[@toilets-sewers|Sewers]] carry dirty water out. Cables carry power. Planners also decide how tall buildings can be and how far apart they must stand, so light and air reach the street. These rules are called zoning. They can also keep noisy, smoky factories away from homes and schools. New York passed one of the first big zoning laws in 1916, after tall towers began blocking out the sun.

When a city grows faster than its plan, the gaps show. Homes go up without drains. Lakes are filled in and then flood. Bengaluru, for example, has struggled with flooding partly because many of its old lakes and the channels between them were built over.

For much of the 20th century, many planners designed cities around the car. Wide roads and flyovers came first. But wider roads tend to attract more cars, and traffic jams return.

Many cities now try a different approach. Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru have built metro lines. Some streets get wider footpaths and cycle lanes. The idea is simple: when homes, schools and jobs are close together and easy to reach on foot or by train, fewer people need to sit in traffic at all.

text: A square root answers the question: which number, multiplied by itself, gives this number? The square root of 25 is 5, because 5 × 5 = 25. The square root of 100 is 10. We write it with a special sign, √, so √25 = 5.

The name comes from squares. If a square has [[@area-volume|an area of 49 tiles]], its sides are √49 = 7 tiles long. Finding a square root is like working backwards from the area of a square to the length of its side. Some numbers, like 2, have square roots whose digits go on forever.

st.prompt: Which whole number is closest to the square root of 50?
st.reveal: 7 × 7 = 49, which is just below 50, so the square root of 50 is a tiny bit more than 7, about 7.07. Halving 50 to get 25 is a common mistake, because a square root is not half.

d.try: Take 36 coins, buttons or small stones and try to arrange them into a perfect square. How many are on each side? Now try 30 of them. You will find you can't make a square, which is why 30 has no whole-number square root.
myth: The square root of a number is half of it.
The square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original. The square root of 16 is 4, not 8. The two match only for 0 and 4: half of 4 is 2, and 2 × 2 = 4.

sec.t:
Numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and 36 are called perfect squares. Their square roots are whole numbers. Most numbers are not like that. √2 is about 1.414. √10 is about 3.162. Their [[@decimals|decimals]] never end.

In ancient Greece, followers of Pythagoras proved that √2 cannot be written as a fraction at all. Numbers like this are called irrational, meaning they can't be written as a ratio of two whole numbers. A legend says a follower named Hippasus was drowned for revealing it, but there is no reliable evidence for the story.

At Yale University in the USA there is a small, round clay tablet called YBC 7289. It comes from ancient Babylon, in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and is thought to date from around 1800 to 1600 BCE. It may have been a student's exercise.

On it is a square with its diagonals drawn in. Next to the diagonal is a number, written in the Babylonian base-60 system, that equals about 1.41421296. That is the square root of 2, correct to about six [[decimal|decimal]] places. The scribe also used it to work out the diagonal of a square with sides of 30.

In India, the Sulba Sutras gave √2 as about 1.4142156, and in 499 CE [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] described a step-by-step method for finding square roots of large numbers.

{{story:calculators}}

How did people find square roots before calculators? One good method is very old, and sometimes called the Babylonian method. Make a guess. Divide the number by your guess. Then take the average of your guess and the answer. That average is a better guess. Repeat.

Try it for √10. Guess 3. 10 ÷ 3 is about 3.33. The average of 3 and 3.33 is about 3.17. Try again with 3.17 and you get about 3.1623, which is almost exactly right. A modern [[@calculators|calculator]] uses clever methods like this, repeated very fast.

Square roots appear whenever squares and distances do. The [[@pythagoras|Pythagorean theorem]] says a² + b² = c², so finding the long side of a triangle means taking a square root. A builder checking a diagonal, a game working out how far apart two characters are, and a phone's GPS all use them.

They also show up in nature and science. [[@how-swings|A pendulum's swing time]] depends on the square root of its length, so a [[pendulum|pendulum]] four times as long swings only twice as slowly. And what about the square root of a negative number, like −1? No ordinary number works, because any number times itself is positive. So mathematicians invented a new one, called *i*. It sounds like make-believe, but engineers use it every day to design electrical [[circuit|circuits]].

text: For a long time, India won very little in boxing. That changed in the 2000s. In 2008, Vijender Singh won India's first Olympic boxing medal, a bronze in Beijing. Four years later, [[@mary-kom|Mary Kom]] won bronze at London 2012, the first Games to include women's boxing.

Since then, Indian women in particular have become a force. Nikhat Zareen, Lovlina Borgohain, Nitu Ghanghas, Saweety Boora, Jaismine Lamboria and Minakshi Hooda have all won world titles. Much of this talent comes from two places: the small town of Bhiwani in Haryana, and Manipur in the [[@northeast-india|Northeast]].

st.reveal: Judges score clean blows with the knuckle part of the glove to the front or sides of the head and body. Defence, footwork and control matter too. Wild swinging that misses earns nothing.

In Olympic-style boxing, points come from clean punches, and speed, timing and defence often beat raw power. Many champions, including Mary Kom, were smaller than their opponents.

sec.t:
Cuba, a small island nation, has won more Olympic boxing golds than almost anyone. So when Bhiwani started producing boxer after boxer, people called it "Mini Cuba". Vijender Singh trained there, and so did many others on India's national team.

Part of the story begins with Hawa Singh, a soldier who won heavyweight gold at the [[@asian-games|Asian Games]] in 1966 and 1970. He later coached in Bhiwani and helped build a boxing culture there. Haryana already loved [[@wrestling-india|wrestling]] and kabaddi. Families saw that sport could lead to government jobs, often in the army or police, and young people lined up at the boxing clubs.

Lovlina Borgohain, from a village in Assam, won bronze at the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021. Nikhat Zareen, from Nizamabad in Telangana, won world titles in 2022 and 2023. At the 2023 World Championships in New Delhi, Indian women won four gold medals.

In September 2025, at the World Boxing Championships in Liverpool, Jaismine Lamboria and Minakshi Hooda both became world champions. Many of these boxers had to argue with relatives or neighbours who thought boxing was no sport for girls. Their medals have changed a lot of minds, and many villages now hold proud welcomes for returning champions.

An Olympic bout lasts three rounds of three minutes each, with a minute's rest between them. Five judges score each round. They reward clean punches that land with the front of the glove, as well as good defence and control of the fight. Boxers are grouped by weight, so a 48 kg flyweight never has to fight someone twice her size. Elite men stopped wearing padded headguards at major amateur events in 2013, after officials argued that the guards gave a false sense of safety.

Boxers need fast [[@reflexes|reflexes]] to slip a punch and fire one back. They skip, run and spar for hours. Boxing can cause [[@sports-injuries|injuries]], especially to the head, which is why rules, gloves, doctors and referees are so strict.

At Paris 2024, India's boxers came home without a medal, a reminder of how hard the Olympics are. But boxing will be at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles, and India now has more young boxers, coaches and training centres than ever. Many of those young boxers are girls who grew up watching Mary Kom on television, the way she once watched Dingko Singh.

text: Playing cards were most likely invented in [[@ancient-china|China]] by about the 9th century CE, during the Tang [[dynasty|dynasty]]. China already had paper and woodblock printing, so making sets of small printed cards was possible.

Cards spread west along trade routes. Players in the Islamic world, especially Mamluk Egypt, made packs with suits of cups, coins, swords and polo sticks. In the 1370s cards reached Europe, where suits changed again into today's hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades. In India they took a different path, becoming the round, hand-painted ganjifa cards of the Mughal courts.

st.prompt: Why did the French suits of hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades spread so widely?

options.t: Their simple shapes were cheap to print with stencils
A French king ordered every country to use them
They were the oldest suits

st.reveal: Earlier suits like cups, coins and swords had detailed pictures. The French shapes could be stencilled in flat red and black, so cards became cheaper to make. Cheap cards travelled further.

d.try: Shuffle a pack of cards well and turn them over one at a time, counting how many cards you turn before the first ace appears. Do it five times and work out the average. Then think about why the answer is usually around ten.
myth: The 52 cards stand for the 52 weeks of the year, and the four suits for the four seasons.
It is a popular idea, but there is no evidence card makers planned it. Packs had different numbers of cards in different places, and 52 became standard slowly, over centuries.
facts: China, by about the 9th century CE

sec.t:
Cards need [[@paper-invention|paper]], and paper was invented in China. A short record from the 9th century mentions members of a princess's family playing a "leaf game", which many historians think was a card game. Early Chinese cards may have been linked to paper money and dice.

By the time cards reached Europe, people there were learning to print with woodblocks too. Some of the earliest European prints were playing cards. The [[@printing-press|printing press]], invented a little later, made them cheaper still.

In India, the [[@mughals|Mughal]] emperors and their courts played ganjifa, a game that came from Persia. Ganjifa cards are round, and were often painted by hand on cloth, ivory, tortoiseshell or lacquered paper. The Mughal pack had eight suits with 12 cards each.

Indian artists created their own versions. Dashavatara ganjifa had ten suits, one for each avatar of Vishnu, from the fish to Kalki. A rich pack could take an artist weeks to paint. Craftspeople in Sawantwadi, in Maharashtra, and in a few other towns still make them by hand.

The court cards in a French-style pack show a king, queen and jack. Old European packs often had only male figures, such as a king and two knights. The queen became standard in France.

The joker arrived much later. It was added in the United States in the 1860s for a game called euchre. Different countries also use different numbers of cards. Some Italian, Spanish and German games use 32, 36 or 40 cards.

Card games mix luck and skill. You cannot choose your cards, but you can choose how to play them. In India, families play games such as rummy and teen patti at weddings and festivals, and the Bengali game of twenty-nine is popular in the east.

A 52-card pack can be shuffled into more possible orders than there are [[atom|atoms]] on Earth, a fact that makes [[@probability|probability]] experts smile. That is why a well-shuffled pack is almost certainly in an order nobody has ever seen before. Magicians use the same pack, along with sleight of hand, to pull off [[@magic-tricks|card tricks]] that seem impossible.

text: A music festival is a gathering where many musicians perform over one or more days, often on several stages. Some are held in fields with tents, food stalls and crowds of tens of thousands. Others take place in concert halls, temple grounds or along river banks.

India and the USA both have famous festivals. In 1969, the Woodstock festival in New York State drew about 400,000 people for three days of rock and folk music. In Chennai, the December Music Season fills dozens of halls with Carnatic music for weeks, as it has since 1927.

st.prompt: At a big outdoor concert, why are there often extra speaker towers far back in the crowd?

options.t: Sound gets quieter and arrives later the farther it travels
To play different songs for people at the back
To stop rain falling on the crowd

st.reveal: Sound spreads out and fades over distance, and it travels at about 343 metres a second. Delay towers are set to play a split second later, so their sound lines up with the sound arriving from the main stage.

d.try: Stand at one end of a playground or long corridor while a friend claps two pieces of wood or two books together at the other end. Watch their hands closely. On a big enough field, you may notice the sound arrives a tiny bit after you see the clap.
myth: Music festivals are a modern Western invention.
People have gathered for days of music for centuries. In India, the Thyagaraja Aradhana has been held in Thiruvaiyaru since the 1800s, and temple festivals with music go back much further.

sec.h: Woodstock and the big field festival
sec.t:
Woodstock was held on a dairy farm in Bethel, New York, and the organisers expected far fewer people than came. About 400,000 turned up. Traffic stopped for kilometres, fences fell, and the organisers gave up selling tickets. It rained, the fields turned to mud, and food ran short.

Even so, the festival was remembered as peaceful, and it became a symbol of the 1960s. In England, the Glastonbury Festival began on a farm in 1970 and now draws around 200,000 people. Festivals like these mix [[@rock-music|rock]], pop, folk and other styles on many stages at once.

In [[@chennai|Chennai]], the Madras Music Academy began holding a December conference in 1927. Today, December and early January are called "the Season". Hundreds of concerts take place in sabhas, or music halls, across the city, many of them free or cheap.

Fans hop from one hall to the next, and the canteens become almost as famous as the concerts. In Pune, the Sawai Gandharva festival, started in 1953 by the singer Bhimsen Joshi, does the same for Hindustani music. Some performances there have gone on all night.

A big stage needs powerful sound equipment. Microphones pick up voices and instruments, a mixing desk balances them, and tall stacks of speakers send sound across the field. Sound fades as it spreads, and it travels at about 343 metres a second, as [[@sound-travel|how sound travels]] explains.

So big festivals put extra speakers, called delay towers, far back in the crowd. They are timed to play a fraction of a second late, so the sound from the stage and the tower arrive together. Without them, people at the back would hear an echo.

A festival is like a small town that pops up for a few days. Organisers plan water taps, toilets, first-aid tents, lost-children points and ways out in an emergency. Some fields are planned weeks ahead, down to where each food stall goes.

Loud music can damage hearing, especially close to the speakers. Many festivals now hand out [[@how-noise-cancel-ears|earplugs]], and children often wear ear defenders. Your [[@ears-hear|ears]] can recover from a little noise, but very loud sound for hours can cause lasting harm. In Nagaland, the [[@india-wonder-hornbill-festival|Hornbill Festival]], held every December since 2000, mixes rock concerts with traditional Naga music and dance.

text: People climb mountains for many reasons: adventure, the view, the challenge, to test themselves, or to stand somewhere few humans have stood. When the British climber George Mallory was asked in 1923 why he wanted to climb Everest, he reportedly answered, "Because it's there."

Mountaineering is the sport of climbing big mountains, often over many days. Climbers use ropes, ice [[axis|axes]] and spiked crampons on their boots. On the highest peaks, the thin air is as big a challenge as the steep rock and ice.

st.prompt: Why do climbers spend weeks going up and down a mountain before trying for the summit?

options.t: To let their bodies slowly adjust to thin air
To carry all their food to the top first
Because the rules say they must

st.reveal: This is called acclimatisation. At high altitude the body makes more red blood cells and breathes faster to get enough oxygen. Going up slowly, then down to sleep, helps prevent altitude sickness, which can be dangerous.

myth: The top of Everest is the furthest point from the centre of the Earth.

Because the Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is further from Earth's centre, even though it is about 2,500 metres lower above sea level. Everest is the highest above sea level.

sec.t:
People have crossed mountain passes for thousands of years, to trade, to pray or to find new land. [[@sport-climbing|Climbing for sport]] began in the Alps. In 1786 two Frenchmen, Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard, reached the top of Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in western Europe. This is often called the start of modern mountaineering.

In the 1800s British climbers raced to climb Alpine peaks. Then attention turned to the Himalaya, where 14 mountains rise above 8,000 metres.

Everest got its English name in 1865, after George Everest, a former head of the Survey of India. In 1852 a Bengali mathematician working for the survey, Radhanath Sikdar, is said to have been the first to calculate that it was the highest peak in the world. In Nepal it is called Sagarmatha, and in Tibet Chomolungma.

Above about 8,000 metres, climbers enter what is called the death zone. The air pressure is so low that each breath holds only about a third of the oxygen at sea level. The body cannot adapt fully, so it slowly weakens. Most climbers carry bottled oxygen.

Climbers first spend weeks acclimatising, climbing to higher camps and returning to sleep lower down. Their bodies make more red [[@blood|blood]] cells. Even so, altitude sickness, frostbite and avalanches make high mountains very dangerous.

Much of the work on Himalayan [[expedition|expeditions]] is done by [[@people-sherpas|Sherpa climbers]] from Nepal, who fix ropes, carry loads and guide clients. Kami Rita Sherpa had climbed Everest 32 times by 2026, more than anyone else.

In 1978 Reinhold Messner of Italy and Peter Habeler of Austria became the first to climb Everest without bottled oxygen. Messner went on to climb all 14 eight-thousanders by 1986.

Today hundreds of people may try to climb Everest each spring, and there have been long queues near the summit. Rubbish, old tents and used oxygen bottles have piled up on the mountain. Nepal and expedition groups now organise clean-up campaigns and require climbers to bring waste down.

You do not need to climb Everest to be a mountaineer. India has many training schools, including the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute in Darjeeling, founded in 1954 with Tenzing as its first director of field training. Many people begin with short treks in the hills of [[@nepal|Nepal]], Himachal or [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], always with trained guides.

text: India has many great sportswomen, across very different sports. Boxer Mary Kom, badminton star PV Sindhu, shooter Manu Bhaker, cricketer Mithali Raj, sprinter PT Usha and chess players Koneru Humpy and Divya Deshmukh are a few of the best known.
They have won Olympic medals, world titles and World Cups. Many came from small towns and families with little money, and some trained with poor equipment for years before anyone noticed them.
In recent years their success has drawn huge crowds and TV audiences. In 2025 India's women's cricket team won the 50-over World Cup, one of the biggest moments in Indian sport.

Indian women have been winning on the world stage for decades. PT Usha won many Asian titles in the 1980s, and Karnam Malleswari won an Olympic medal in 2000. What has grown recently is the attention, money and number of girls taking part.

sec.h: Pioneers on the track and in the gym
sec.t:
PT Usha, from Kerala, was the queen of Indian athletics in the 1980s. She won a string of gold medals at the Asian Games and Asian Championships. At the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics she finished fourth in the 400 m hurdles, missing bronze by one hundredth of a second.

In 2000, weightlifter Karnam Malleswari, from Andhra Pradesh, won bronze at the Sydney Olympics. She became the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal. In 2003 long jumper Anju Bobby George won bronze at the World Championships in Paris, India's first medal at that event.

[[@mary-kom|Mary Kom]] grew up in a farming family in Manipur. She took up boxing as a teenager and went on to win six world championships. In 2012, when women's boxing joined the Olympics, she won bronze in London, even though she had to box in a heavier class than her usual one.

Badminton gave India two Olympic stars. Saina Nehwal won bronze in 2012. Then [[@pv-sindhu|PV Sindhu]], from Hyderabad, won silver in 2016 and bronze in 2021, becoming the first Indian woman with two Olympic medals. Sindhu is also a world champion, from 2019.

sec.h: On target and over the board
sec.t:
Shooting has brought India many medals. At the Paris Olympics in 2024, Manu Bhaker won two bronze medals, one alone and one in a mixed team event. She became the first Indian to win two medals at a single Olympics since independence.

Weightlifter Mirabai Chanu won silver at Tokyo in 2021. Boxer Lovlina Borgohain and wrestler Sakshi Malik have also won Olympic medals.

In [[@chess-india|chess]], a game with roots in India, Koneru Humpy has been one of the world's top women players for over two decades. In 2025, two Indians, Humpy and 19-year-old Divya Deshmukh, met in the final of the Women's World Cup. Divya won and earned the title of [[grandmaster|grandmaster]].

Many of these athletes faced extra hurdles because they were women. Some were told sport wasn't for girls. Others had to fight for equal pay, decent coaching or safe places to train.

Their wins have changed things. More girls now play cricket in school, box in local clubs and enter chess [[tournament|tournaments]]. In the USA, stars like Serena Williams and Simone Biles inspired a generation. In India, a girl watching Sindhu or Harmanpreet on TV can now see someone who looks like her lifting a trophy.

text: Smells are tiny invisible particles floating in the air. When you breathe in, some of them drift to a small patch high up inside your nose, about the size of a postage stamp. It's covered in millions of nerve cells with tiny hairs that poke into a layer of [[mucus|mucus]].

Those hairs carry [[receptor|receptors]], little docking stations that catch particular kinds of smell [[molecule|molecules]]. Humans have about 400 different kinds. When a molecule docks, the nerve cell fires a signal straight up into the brain.
Most smells are made of many different molecules at once. Your brain reads the pattern of which receptors fire, a bit like recognising a song from its notes, and names the smell.

st.prompt: Which of these animals has the most genes for smell receptors?

options.t: African elephant
Dog
Human

st.reveal: The African elephant, with about 2,000. Dogs have about 800, and humans about 400 that work. Elephants use their trunks to sniff out water, food and each other from far away.

n.certNote: How smell works is well understood. How many different smells a person can tell apart is disputed. One 2014 study suggested about a trillion, but other scientists argued its maths was flawed.

myth: Humans have a terrible sense of smell compared with other animals.

Humans can smell some things as well as dogs can, and better than many animals. A neuroscientist reviewing the evidence in 2017 traced the idea back to the 1800s, when a French scientist assumed our small smell area meant a weak sense.

sec.t:
Signals from your nose go first to a part of the brain called the olfactory bulb. From there they pass close to the areas that handle emotions and [[@memory|memories]]. That's why a smell can bring back a memory so strongly. The scent of agarbatti, of a grandmother's kitchen, or of a new school book can take you back years in a single breath.

Other senses take a longer route through the brain before reaching those areas. Shops and hotels know this, and some pump gentle scents into their lobbies to put customers in a good mood.

sec.h: Not as bad as we thought
sec.t:
People often say humans have a poor sense of smell. In 2017, an American neuroscientist named John McGann looked at the evidence and found this was mostly a myth from the 1800s. In tests, people can follow a scent trail across a field, a bit like a dog. We're especially good at some smells, like the scent of a banana.

[[@dogs-domestic|Dogs]] are still far better at many smells. They have many more smell cells than we do, which is why they're trained to sniff out lost people and hidden things at airports. Elephants may be champions, with more smell [[gene|genes]] than any animal tested.

Your nose also warms and moistens the air you breathe, and its hairs and mucus trap dust and germs. A sudden tickle can set off a [[@sneezes|sneeze]], blasting out whatever is irritating it.

Smell keeps you safe too. Cooking gas has almost no smell of its own, so gas companies add a strong-smelling chemical. If there's a leak, your nose warns you.

A cold can block smell for a few days. Some people lose their sense of smell for longer, for example after certain [[infection|infections]] such as COVID-19. Food then tastes flat, because flavour depends so much on smell. Doctors sometimes suggest "smell training", sniffing a few strong scents every day, and the nose's smell cells are replaced every month or two, which may help some people recover.

text: Staying safe online mostly comes down to [[@habits|a few habits]]. Keep personal details private, such as your full name, address, school, phone number and passwords. Be careful about who you talk to, because people online aren't always who they say they are. Think before you click links or download files, especially from surprise messages. And if anything makes you feel worried, scared or uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult.

None of this means the [[@internet-how|internet]] is a bad place. It is where people learn, play, create and stay in touch. Safety habits are like looking both ways before crossing a road: quick, simple and worth doing every time.

st.prompt: A message says you've won a new phone and just need to click a link and enter your parent's bank details. What is it most likely to be?

options.t: A phishing scam trying to steal information
A real prize from a company
A test from your school

st.reveal: Real prizes don't ask for bank details or passwords through a surprise message. Scammers use exciting offers or scary warnings to make people act fast without thinking. The safest move is not to click, and to show the message to a trusted adult.

d.try: With a parent or teacher, look at the privacy settings on an app or game you use. Find out who can see your profile, who can message you and whether your location is shared. Change anything you're not comfortable with together. It takes ten minutes and helps a lot.
myth: Using private or incognito mode makes you invisible online.
Incognito mode only stops your browser saving your history and cookies on that device. The websites you visit, your school or workplace network and your internet provider can still see your activity.

sec.t:
Some information can be used to find you in real life, or to pretend to be you. Your home address, school name, phone number and daily routine fall into this group. So do photos that show your school uniform or the street sign outside your house.

Your [[@passwords|passwords]] and one-time codes are private too, even from friends. A friend today might be a former friend next year, and some "friends" online are strangers. Sharing a password with a parent or guardian is different, because they're responsible for keeping you safe.

Many online dangers are tricks rather than hacking. Phishing messages pretend to come from a bank, a game company or a friend, and ask you to click a link or share details. They often try to rush you, with warnings that your account will be deleted or news that you've won a prize.

Warning signs include spelling mistakes, strange web addresses, [[@tech-spam-email|offers that seem too good to be true]], and requests for passwords, codes or money. In India, some scammers phone people pretending to be from a bank and ask for the OTP sent to their phone. Real [[@money-banks|banks]] never ask for it. The government runs a national cybercrime helpline, 1930, and a website for reporting fraud.

sec.h: People are not always who they seem

sec.t:
[[@cyberbullying|Cyberbullying]] means using messages, posts or games to hurt or embarrass someone, often again and again. It can feel worse than other bullying because it follows you home on your phone.

If it happens to you, don't reply to [[@bullying|the bully]]. Take screenshots as a record, block the person and report them using the app's tools. Then tell an adult you trust. If you see it happening to someone else, a kind message to them, or a report, can help.

Remember too that not everything you see online is true. Learning to spot [[@fake-news|false information]] is part of staying safe.

Most big [[@social-media|social media]] apps say users must be at least 13. This comes largely from a US law that limits how companies can [[@app-safety|collect data]] from younger children. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 says companies need a parent's permission before handling the personal data of anyone under 18.

Time matters as well as safety. Long hours online, especially late at night, can affect sleep and mood, as [[@screen-time|screen time]] research shows. Many families agree simple rules together, such as no phones at meals or in bedrooms at night.

text: Dadabhai Naoroji was a teacher, businessman, writer and politician from Bombay. He spent more than 60 years arguing that British rule was draining India's wealth, and he backed his case with numbers rather than slogans. He helped found the Indian National Congress in 1885 and led it three times.

In 1892 he became a member of the British House of Commons, the heart of the government that ruled India. He is usually remembered as the first Indian elected to it. That gave Indians a voice inside Parliament for the first time, and it is why people still call him the Grand Old Man of India.

sec.t:
Naoroji was born in 1825 into a poor Parsi family. His father died when he was a small child, and his mother worked hard to keep him in school. He was a brilliant student at Elphinstone College in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], then called Bombay, and later became a professor of mathematics there. He was one of the first Indians to hold such a post.

He also cared about girls' education at a time when few girls went to school. With friends, he helped open schools for girls in Bombay in the 1840s, and he started a Gujarati newspaper, *Rast Goftar*, which argued for social reform. Later, in 1874, he served for a short time as diwan, or chief minister, of Baroda, one of the princely states ruled by Indian kings under British control. He tried to clean up its government but left after disagreements within a year.

Naoroji decided that the best place to argue was inside Parliament itself. In 1886 he lost his first election. Two years later, Britain's prime minister, Lord Salisbury, said in a speech that British voters would not elect a "black man". The insult backfired. Many British people were shocked, and Naoroji became famous across [[@london|London]].

In 1892 he stood in Finsbury Central, a working-class area of London, and won by just five votes. He took his oath on the Khordeh Avesta, his Zoroastrian holy book. In Parliament he spoke about Indian poverty, unfair taxes and the need for Indians to hold top government jobs. He lost his seat in 1895, but he had made his point.

By the time he presided over the Congress session in Calcutta in 1906, Naoroji was over 80. His message had sharpened. India, he said, needed swaraj, or self-government. It was one of the first times the demand was made so plainly from that platform.

He also inspired a younger generation. A young lawyer named Gandhi wrote to him for advice from South Africa, where Gandhi was fighting unfair laws. Later leaders built the [[@swadeshi|swadeshi]] movement partly on his idea that India's wealth should stay in India.

Naoroji died in Bombay in 1917, thirty years before India became independent. A street in London's Finsbury is named after him.

text: The Statue of Unity is a giant statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the leader who helped bring more than 560 [[@princely-states|princely states]] together to form India in 1947. It stands 182 m tall on a small river island near Kevadia in Gujarat, now also called Ekta Nagar.

It is the tallest statue in the world. That is about as tall as a 60-storey building, and around 18 times the height of a three-storey school. It shows Patel walking, wearing a simple shawl over his kurta, and looking towards the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada river. It opened on his birthday, 31 October 2018.

It is mostly hollow. Inside is a frame of steel and reinforced concrete, with lifts and a viewing gallery. The outside is covered with bronze panels.

sec.h: Why Patel, and why so big?
sec.t:
[[@sardar-patel|Sardar Patel]] is remembered as the Iron Man of India. As the country's first Home Minister, he persuaded rulers of princely states to join India, which gave the country much of its present shape. The statue's name honours that work.

The idea was announced in 2010 by the Gujarat government. Planners wanted something people would travel to see, like the Statue of Liberty in New York. The location had a link too. Patel is often credited with first backing the idea of a big dam on the Narmada, and the statue now overlooks it.

The design came from Ram V. Sutar, a sculptor then in his late eighties who had made hundreds of statues of Indian leaders. He started with small models, studied old photographs of Patel, and scaled them up.

Building a statue this size is closer to building a skyscraper than carving a [[sculpture|sculpture]]. The core is two tall towers of reinforced concrete, inside a steel frame. Around this frame is a skin of bronze panels, each one cast separately and fitted together. The panels were cast in China and shipped to India, which caused some argument at the time.

{{story:bronze-casting}}

Engineers designed it to survive powerful winds and [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]]. A statue is harder to build than a tower because it is not a neat shape. The legs, for example, had to be made wide apart and strong enough to hold everything above them. Around 3,000 workers and engineers took about four years to finish it.

Before construction began, organisers ran a campaign asking farmers across India to donate old iron farm tools, such as worn-out ploughs. The idea was that every village could add a little to the statue of the man who united the country. Many thousands of villages took part.

The [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]] is 93 m tall including its stone pedestal, so the Statue of Unity is about twice its height. Before 2018, the tallest statue was the Spring Temple Buddha in Henan, China, at about 128 m.

At 182 m, the Statue of Unity is taller than the Qutub Minar in [[@delhi|Delhi]], about 73 m, stacked twice.

Supporters say the statue honours a national hero and has brought jobs and tourists to a quiet tribal region. Several million people visit every year. Around it have grown gardens, a safari park and other attractions.

Critics have raised other points. The project cost about ₹3,000 crore, and some argued that money could have gone to schools or farms. Some Adivasi (tribal) families living nearby said they lost land or were not consulted fairly. These debates happen around many giant projects, from [[@dams-power|dams]] to highways.

At night, the statue is lit up, and a laser and sound show tells Patel's story on the side of the dam. It ends, as many visits do, with people craning their necks to see the top.

text: The highest air temperature ever officially recorded is 56.7 °C (134 °F), measured at Furnace Creek in Death Valley, California, on 10 July 1913. That is hot enough that a metal car door handle left in the sun could burn your hand.

But [[@weather-records|"hottest place"]] can mean different things. It might mean the highest air temperature on one day, the hottest ground, or the place that is hottest all year round. Each has a different winner. And because old records were taken with simple instruments, scientists still argue about some of them.

st.prompt: Where are official air temperatures measured?

options.t: In the shade, in a ventilated box above the ground
On the ground in full sunlight
On the roof of the tallest building in town

st.reveal: Weather instruments sit in shaded, airy boxes, usually 1.25 to 2 m above grass. That measures the air itself, not the sunshine. In direct sun, a thermometer can read much higher.

n.certNote: The World Meteorological Organization accepts 56.7 °C at Death Valley in 1913 as the world record. Some weather historians argue that the 1913 reading was faulty, which would make a 54.4 °C reading from Death Valley in 2020 or 2021 among the highest reliable measurements.

That reading, from 1922, was the official record for 90 years. In 2012, a World Meteorological Organization panel found problems with how it was measured and threw it out.

sec.t:
Death Valley is a long, deep desert valley in eastern California. Parts of it lie below sea level, the lowest at about 86 m below. Hot air gets trapped between the steep mountains on either side, and the dark, bare ground soaks up sunshine and heats the air further.

Summers there regularly pass 50 °C. In 2020 and 2021, it reached about 54.4 °C, among the highest temperatures reliably measured anywhere. Some weather historians think the 1913 record was a mistake, and that these newer readings may be the true highest. Others accept the old record. The question is still open.

sec.h: The record that was thrown out

sec.t:
Air temperature is measured in the shade. The ground in full sun gets much hotter. NASA satellites have measured land surface temperatures of around 70 °C in the Lut Desert of Iran, a region of dark rock and sand.

At Dallol, in Ethiopia, the average temperature over a whole year was measured at about 34 °C in the 1960s, one of the highest averages known for any inhabited place. Dallol also has bubbling [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]], [[acid|acid]] pools and salt crusts in yellow, green and orange.

India's official record is 51 °C, measured at Phalodi in Rajasthan on 19 May 2016. Churu, also in Rajasthan, reached 50.8 °C in 2019. Before [[@monsoon|the monsoon]] arrives, much of north and central India can swelter above 45 °C for days at a time.

Heat is harder on the body when the air is also humid. Your body cools itself by [[@sweat|sweating]], and the [[@body-temperature|sweat]] needs to evaporate. In very humid air it can't, which is why a 38 °C day in Chennai can feel worse than a 42 °C day in [[@jaipur|Jaipur]]. Drinking enough [[@water-drink|water]] and staying in the shade really do matter.

As the [[climate|climate]] warms, record-breaking [[@heatwaves|heatwaves]] are becoming more common, as explained in [[@climate-change|climate change]]. But Earth's hottest places are still mild compared with other spots in the [[solar-system|solar system]].

The surface of Venus is about 465 °C, hot enough to melt lead, as you can read in [[@venus-hot|Venus]]. The surface of the Sun is about 5,500 °C. [[@what-if-hole-through-earth|Deep inside the Earth]], the core is thought to be about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

text: Tamil Nadu's temple towers are part of a building style called Dravidian [[architecture|architecture]]. The tallest are usually gopurams, gateway towers over the entrances. Over many centuries, kings and communities kept expanding their favourite temples, adding new walls around the old ones. Each new wall got a bigger, grander gateway than the last.

The towers had several jobs. They marked the boundary of sacred ground. They could be seen from far across flat farmland, guiding pilgrims in. And they showed the power and generosity of whoever paid for them. Their steps are covered with thousands of painted figures of gods, goddesses, animals and stories, so a tower is also a giant [[@picture-books|picture book]].

st.prompt: In big temples like Madurai's Meenakshi Temple, where are the tallest towers?

options.t: At the outer gateways, on the edges of the temple
Directly over the inner shrine
In the very centre of the courtyard

st.reveal: As temples grew, rulers added new walls around the old ones, each with grander gateways. The outer gopurams ended up tallest, while the shrine at the centre stayed smaller and older.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples.

myth: The huge stone on top of the Thanjavur temple was raised up a ramp 6 km long.

This story is popular and often repeated, but there is no clear evidence for it. Nobody knows exactly how the builders lifted the capstone, and historians and engineers have suggested several methods.

sec.h: When gateways grew taller than shrines
sec.t:
In the Chola temples, the tallest tower sat over the shrine. Later, from about the 1200s onwards, things changed. Rulers including the Pandyas, the kings of [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] and the Nayakas who governed for them poured money into gateways instead.

Temples grew outwards in rings, like the layers of an onion. Each ring had high walls and four gopurams, one on each side. The outermost gopurams became the tallest of all, while the old shrine in the middle stayed comparatively small. Walking in, you pass through gateway after gateway, from the noisy street towards the quiet centre.

The [[@meenakshi-temple|Meenakshi Temple]] in Madurai has 14 gopurams, the tallest about 52 m high. They're covered with brightly painted figures, and are repainted from time to time during big renovation ceremonies. Inside, a hall of carved pillars and a large temple tank draw crowds every day.

At Srirangam, near Tiruchirappalli, the Ranganathaswamy Temple is one of the largest working temple complexes in India, with seven rings of walls. Its main gateway, the Rajagopuram, was left unfinished for centuries and only completed in 1987. It rises about 73 m, roughly as tall as a 20-storey building.

sec.h: Built to last, and to be used
sec.t:
Gopurams are mostly brick and plaster on a stone base, which kept them lighter than solid stone. Their stepped shape, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, makes them steady, like a pyramid. The upper levels are often hollow inside. At the very top runs a barrel-shaped roof lined with a row of pot-shaped finials, called kalasams, which catch the sunlight from far away.

These temples are living places. Musicians play, priests carry out daily [[ritual|rituals]], and festivals pull huge wooden chariots through the streets. Many famous [[@bronze-casting|bronze]] statues were made to be carried in such processions. Even the state's official emblem shows a gopuram, a sign of how closely the towers are linked to Tamil identity.

text: Idli and dosa batter is made by soaking rice and urad dal, grinding them into a thick paste, and leaving it overnight. While the kitchen sleeps, [[microbe|microbes]] in the batter wake up and feed.

Lactic [[acid|acid]] [[bacteria|bacteria]] turn some of the sugars into acid, which gives the batter its gentle sour taste. Bacteria and yeasts also give off bubbles of carbon dioxide gas, so by morning the batter has risen and is full of [[@food-why-cheese-holes|tiny holes]]. Steam it and you get soft, spongy idlis. Spread it thin on a hot griddle and you get a crisp dosa. Without the overnight wait, both would come out flat and heavy.

st.prompt: Idli batter rises much faster in Chennai in May than in Delhi in January. Why?

options.t: The microbes in the batter work faster when it is warm
Rice grown in the south has more gas in it
Cold air pushes down on the batter

st.reveal: Bacteria and yeasts are living things, and like most living things they slow down in the cold. In a warm kitchen, batter can double overnight. In winter, cooks often keep it in a warm spot or wait a few extra hours.

n.certNote: The science of fermentation is well understood. Where idli first came from is debated. Some historians think the steaming method arrived from Indonesia, while others think it grew up in South India.

d.try: Next time someone at home grinds idli or dosa batter, stick a strip of tape on the outside of the container to mark the level. Check again the next morning and measure how far it rose. Smell it too. The sour smell comes from acid made by the microbes.
myth: Fermented food is just food that has started to go bad.

Spoiling is caused by unwanted microbes. Fermentation is controlled growth of helpful ones, which make the food sour, which in turn keeps many harmful germs away. Curd, bread, cheese and idli all depend on it.
facts: often about 3 or 4 parts rice to 1 part dal
about 8–12 hours, longer in cold weather
steamed; dosa is fried on a griddle

sec.t:
Rice alone would not rise well. Urad dal, a small black lentil that is white once its skin is removed, contains a slippery, gummy substance. When it is ground, this goo forms a sticky web in the batter.

That web traps the gas bubbles the way [[gluten|gluten]] does in wheat bread. Cooks say the dal should be ground until it is fluffy and light, almost like whipped cream, and many grind it separately from the rice for this reason. Dal also adds [[protein|protein]], so a plate of idli with sambar is a well-balanced meal.

[[fermentation|Fermentation]] partly breaks down the starch and proteins before you eat them. That is one reason idli is a common first food for babies and a gentle meal for people who are unwell. Studies have found that fermentation can raise the amounts of some B [[@vitamins|vitamins]] in the batter.

Steaming adds no oil at all. A typical idli is light, which is why it is a [[@indian-breakfasts|favourite breakfast]] in hospitals and homes from [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] to New Jersey.

Dosai, an early form of dosa, appears in Tamil writing from well over a thousand years ago, according to the food historian K.T. Achaya. The first clear mention of idli, called *iddalige*, is in a Kannada text written in 920 CE. But that early idli seems to have been made from dal alone and not fermented.

Achaya suggested that the fermented, steamed idli may have come from [[@bali|Indonesia]], where similar steamed cakes were made, perhaps carried by traders or cooks between the 8th and 12th centuries. Other historians are not convinced. What is clear is that by a few hundred years ago, the rice-and-dal idli had become South India's own.

Udupi in coastal Karnataka is famous for its [[@restaurants-history|vegetarian restaurants]], and cooks from there opened eateries across India in the 20th century. Masala dosa, a crisp dosa wrapped around spiced potato, became a favourite in [[@chennai|Chennai]], Mumbai and far beyond.

Today you can buy ready-made batter in packets in Indian shops in Singapore, London and Texas. Even so, the morning check of the rising batter, with a lifted lid and a quick sniff, is a ritual in millions of homes.

text: A laddoo is a ball of flour, seeds or grated coconut, held together with ghee and sugar or [[@jaggery|jaggery]]. It is cheap to make in big batches, easy to share, and it stays good for days without a fridge. That made it perfect for festivals, when a family might feed dozens of guests and send sweets to every neighbour.

Laddoos also carry meaning. In Hindu tradition, the laddoo and its cousin the modak are Lord Ganesha's favourite sweets. Laddoos are handed out at weddings, after exam results and when a baby is born. Saying "laddoo" in many Indian homes is a short way of saying "good news".

st.prompt: Before fridges, why were laddoos a smart sweet to make for a festival?

options.t: Ghee and sugar help them stay good for days
Round sweets cannot go bad
They were only made in cold winter months

st.reveal: Laddoos are fairly dry, and sugar and ghee slow down the growth of microbes. So families could make big batches days ahead, store them in tins and share them with guests over a whole festival week.

myth: Laddoos are just festival treats and were never meant to be everyday food.
Some laddoos are traditional everyday foods. Gond, methi and dry-fruit laddoos are made in many homes in winter, and are often given to new mothers to help them build strength.
facts: besan, boondi, motichoor, til, coconut, rava
flour or seeds, ghee, sugar or jaggery

sec.t:
Before fridges, food spoiled quickly in Indian summers. Laddoos solved that. They contain little water, and sugar and ghee slow down the [[microbe|microbes]] that make food go bad. A tin of besan laddoos can last a week or more.

Ghee and sugar were once expensive luxuries. Making a plate of laddoos was a way to say "this day matters". Each region has its own version. Til laddoos made with sesame and jaggery are eaten at Makar Sankranti in January. Motichoor laddoos, built from hundreds of tiny fried drops of batter, turn up at Diwali and weddings. In Kerala and Tamil Nadu, coconut laddoos are common.

The round shape helps too. A ball has no corners to crumble, packs neatly into a box and fits in one hand, which is useful when you are eating standing up in a crowd.

sec.h: The laddoo with its own passport

sec.t:
Every year during [[@ganesh-chaturthi|Ganesh Chaturthi]], people in Balapur, on the edge of Hyderabad, auction the giant laddoo offered to their Ganesha. The tradition began in 1994, when a local farmer won it for 450 rupees. Bids climbed year after year. In 2026, the winning bid was 39 lakh rupees, about 8,600 times the first price.

Buyers believe the laddoo brings good luck, and the money goes to local causes. Other neighbourhoods in Hyderabad now hold their own auctions, sometimes for even bigger sums.

Nobody knows for certain. The word comes from old Sanskrit names for round sweets. One popular story says the ancient physician Sushruta rolled sesame, jaggery and peanuts into balls to help patients take medicine. That story is told often, but historians have found little solid evidence for it.

What we do know is that ball-shaped sweets have been made across India for many centuries. Cooks used whatever grew nearby: sesame in the north, coconut in the south, rice flour in Bengal and Odisha. Laddoos made with millets are coming back too, as people look for older grains.

There is a bit of maths hiding in every laddoo. Of all shapes, a sphere holds the most stuff inside for the least outside surface. That is why a laddoo dries out slowly, and why soap bubbles and raindrops pull themselves into [[@circles|round shapes]] too.
